## 1. Overview

**BKwG** implements the beta Kumaraswamy-G (BKw-G) family of distributions
introduced by Handique, Chakraborty and Ali (2017). The family places the
Kumaraswamy-G construction of Cordeiro and de Castro (2011) inside the
beta-generated construction of Eugene, Lee and Famoye (2002). Starting from
any continuous baseline distribution $G$, it adds four positive shape
parameters $a$, $b$, $\alpha$ and $\beta$ that control skewness, tail weight
and the shape of the hazard rate.

The package provides

* density, distribution, quantile, random generation, survival, hazard and
  cumulative hazard functions for twelve built-in baselines and for any
  baseline defined by the user;
* the full model and six nested sub-models;
* six estimation methods, with any parameter held fixed;
* likelihood-ratio and Wald tests, goodness-of-fit statistics with
  parametric-bootstrap p-values and model comparison tables;
* moments, the moment generating function, entropies, mean residual life,
  order statistics, the analytical score and the mixture representation.

This vignette walks through each of these in turn.

```{r load}
library(BKwG)
```

## 2. The family

Let $G(x)$ and $g(x)$ be the cdf and pdf of the baseline distribution and let

$$K(x) = 1 - \{1 - G(x)^{a}\}^{b}$$

be the Kumaraswamy-G cdf. The BKw-G distribution has cdf and pdf

$$F(x) = I_{K(x)}(\alpha, \beta), \qquad
  f(x) = \frac{a\, b\, g(x)\, G(x)^{a-1}\{1 - G(x)^{a}\}^{b\beta - 1}
         K(x)^{\alpha-1}}{B(\alpha, \beta)},$$

where $I_y(\alpha, \beta)$ is the regularised incomplete beta function. The
quantile function has the closed form

$$Q(u) = G^{-1}\Big(\big[1 - \{1 - z_u\}^{1/b}\big]^{1/a}\Big),$$

with $z_u$ the $u$-quantile of a Beta$(\alpha, \beta)$ distribution. In the
notation of Handique et al. (2017), `alpha` $= m$ and `beta` $= n$.

### Baselines

Every function takes a `baseline` (a name or an object created by
`bkwg_baseline()`) and `par`, the baseline parameters, given by name or in
the order of the table below.

```{r baselines}
bkwg_baselines()
```

### Sub-models

Fixing some shape parameters at one gives well-known families:

```{r submodels}
bkwg_submodels()
```

## 3. Distribution functions

All functions follow the usual R naming scheme: `d`, `p`, `q`, `r` for the
density, cdf, quantile function and random generation, plus `s`, `h` and
`ch` for the survival, hazard and cumulative hazard.

```{r dpqr}
x <- c(0.5, 1, 2)
dbkwg(x, a = 2, b = 0.7, alpha = 1.6, beta = 2.3,
      baseline = "weibull", par = c(shape = 1.5, scale = 2))
pbkwg(x, 2, 0.7, 1.6, 2.3, par = c(1.5, 2))
qbkwg(c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9), 2, 0.7, 1.6, 2.3, par = c(1.5, 2))
hbkwg(x, 2, 0.7, 1.6, 2.3, par = c(1.5, 2))
```

The computations are done on the log scale, so both tails keep full
precision:

```{r tails}
pbkwg(40, 2, 0.7, 1.6, 2.3, par = c(1.5, 2), lower.tail = FALSE,
      log.p = TRUE)
```

The quantile function and the cdf are inverses of each other, and with
$a = b = \alpha = \beta = 1$ the baseline itself is recovered:

```{r checks}
u <- c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95)
pbkwg(qbkwg(u, 2, 0.7, 1.6, 2.3, par = c(1.5, 2)), 2, 0.7, 1.6, 2.3,
      par = c(1.5, 2))
all.equal(dbkwg(x, par = c(shape = 2, scale = 3)),
          dweibull(x, shape = 2, scale = 3))
```

### Shapes of the density and the hazard

`plot_bkwg()` draws the pdf, cdf, survival function or hazard. The extra
parameters let a Weibull baseline produce densities with very different
skewness, and hazards that are increasing, decreasing, bathtub-shaped or
upside-down bathtub-shaped.

```{r shapes, fig.height = 3.6}
op_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plot_bkwg(2, 1, 1.5, 2, par = c(2, 1), to = 3, main = "Density")
plot_bkwg(0.5, 3, 2, 0.5, par = c(2, 1), from = 0.01, to = 3, add = TRUE,
          col = 2)
plot_bkwg(4, 0.5, 0.6, 1.5, par = c(1, 1), to = 3, add = TRUE, col = 4)
plot_bkwg(0.2, 0.3, 0.8, 1, par = c(3, 1), what = "hazard", from = 0.02,
          to = 2.5, ylim = c(0, 4), main = "Hazard")       # bathtub
plot_bkwg(2, 1, 1.5, 2, par = c(2, 1), what = "hazard", from = 0.02,
          to = 2.5, add = TRUE, col = 2)                   # increasing
plot_bkwg(0.5, 1, 0.5, 1, par = c(1, 1), what = "hazard", from = 0.02,
          to = 2.5, add = TRUE, col = 4)                   # decreasing
plot_bkwg(3, 2, 1, 1, par = c(0.6, 1), what = "hazard", from = 0.02,
          to = 2.5, add = TRUE, col = 3)                   # upside-down bathtub
par(op_par)
```

## 4. Structural properties

Moments, entropies and the other properties are computed by numerical
integration over the quantile function, so they are available for every
baseline.

```{r properties}
mbkwg(1:4, 2, 1, 1.5, 2, par = c(2, 1))
bkwg_stats(2, 1, 1.5, 2, par = c(2, 1))
entropy_bkwg(2, 1, 1.5, 2, par = c(2, 1))
entropy_bkwg(2, 1, 1.5, 2, par = c(2, 1), type = "renyi", delta = 0.5)
mrl_bkwg(c(0.5, 1), 2, 1, 1.5, 2, par = c(2, 1))
```

Order statistics: the density of the maximum and the cdf of the minimum of a
sample of size ten.

```{r order}
dos_bkwg(1, i = 10, N = 10, 2, 1, 1.5, 2, par = c(2, 1))
pos_bkwg(1, i = 1, N = 10, 2, 1, 1.5, 2, par = c(2, 1))
```

The BKw-G density is an infinite mixture of Kumaraswamy-G densities,

$$f(x) = \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} w_j\, f_{\mathrm{KwG}}\{x;\, a, b(\beta + j)\},$$

and `bkwg_mixture()` returns the weights $w_j$:

```{r mixture}
head(bkwg_mixture(alpha = 2.5, beta = 1.5, J = 50))
```

## 5. Estimation

`fit_bkwg()` fits the full model or any sub-model by maximum likelihood
(`"mle"`), maximum product of spacings (`"mps"`), minimum Anderson-Darling
(`"ad"`) or Cramér-von Mises (`"cvm"`) distance, or ordinary (`"lse"`) and
weighted (`"wlse"`) least squares. Any parameter can be fixed through
`fixed =`.

As a first example, a sample is drawn from a Kumaraswamy-exponential
distribution with $a = 2$ and $b = 1.5$, and the two shape parameters are
estimated with the exponential rate held at its known value. (Why the rate is
fixed here is explained in the note on identifiability below.)

```{r fit}
set.seed(123)
y <- rbkwg(300, a = 2, b = 1.5, baseline = "exp", par = c(rate = 1))
fit <- fit_bkwg(y, baseline = "exp", submodel = "KwG", fixed = c(rate = 1))
summary(fit)
confint(fit, type = "log")
```

Fitted objects have the usual methods: `coef()`, `vcov()`, `logLik()`,
`AIC()`, `BIC()`, `nobs()`, `confint()`, `residuals()`, `quantile()` and
`plot()`.

```{r fitplot, fig.height = 5.5}
plot(fit)
```

All six methods give similar answers on this sample:

```{r methods}
meth <- c("mle", "mps", "ad", "cvm", "lse", "wlse")
est <- sapply(meth, function(m)
  coef(fit_bkwg(y, baseline = "exp", submodel = "KwG", method = m,
                fixed = c(rate = 1), hessian = FALSE)))
round(est, 3)
```

### A note on identifiability

The full five- or six-parameter model is flexible but can be weakly
identified. When $\alpha = 1$, $b$ and $\beta$ enter only through the product
$b\beta$. Scale-type baseline parameters can be confounded with the shape
parameters too: for an exponential or Weibull baseline with $a = 1$,
$\{1 - G(x)\}^{b}$ is again exponential or Weibull, so $b$ and the scale cannot
be told apart. Fitting the Kumaraswamy-exponential model above with a free
rate gives a slightly higher likelihood, but estimates far from the true
values $a = 2$, $b = 1.5$ and rate $= 1$:

```{r ident}
fit_free <- fit_bkwg(y, baseline = "exp", submodel = "KwG")
coef(fit_free)
c(free = logLik(fit_free), fixed = logLik(fit))
```

 On some samples the likelihood keeps increasing towards the
boundary of the parameter space (for example $\alpha \to \infty$ with
$\beta \to 0$). The signs are estimates of extreme size, very large standard
errors, or a warning that the information matrix could not be inverted. In
that case, fix a scale parameter or choose a sub-model with `lrt_bkwg()` or
`compare_bkwg()`.

## 6. Hypothesis tests and goodness of fit

Because the sub-models are interior restrictions, likelihood-ratio statistics
have the usual $\chi^2$ limit. `lrt_bkwg()` refits the sub-model itself, and
`wald_bkwg()` gives the joint Wald test. Both return `"htest"` objects.

```{r tests}
lrt_bkwg(fit, "EG")                       # H0: b = 1
wald_bkwg(fit, c(b = 1))
lrt_bkwg(fit, "G")                        # H0: a = b = 1, plain exponential
```

`gof_bkwg()` reports the Cramér-von Mises $W^*$ and Anderson-Darling $A^*$
statistics of Chen and Balakrishnan (1995) and the Kolmogorov-Smirnov
statistic. With `B > 0`, p-values come from a parametric bootstrap that
re-estimates the model on every simulated sample.

```{r gof}
gof_bkwg(fit)
```

```{r gofboot, eval = FALSE}
gof_bkwg(fit, B = 500, seed = 1)          # bootstrap p-values (slower)
```

## 7. Model comparison on real data

The annual precipitation (inches) of 70 US cities, `datasets::precip`, is
fitted with several sub-models and baselines. `compare_bkwg()` returns the
table usually reported when a new distribution is introduced, sorted by AIC.
Standard errors are not needed for the table, so `hessian = FALSE` (passed on
to `fit_bkwg()`) saves time.

```{r compare}
tab <- compare_bkwg(precip, baseline = c("weibull", "gamma"),
                    submodels = c("KwG", "EG", "G"), hessian = FALSE)
tab
```

Each fitted model is kept in the `"fits"` attribute:

```{r best}
best <- attr(tab, "fits")[[tab$model[1]]]
coef(best)
```

## 8. User-defined baselines

Any continuous distribution can be used as the baseline. Only the cdf and the
pdf are needed. A quantile function is optional (otherwise it is found by
numerical inversion). Accepting `lower.tail`/`log.p` in the cdf and `log` in
the pdf improves accuracy in the tails.

```{r custom}
rayleigh <- bkwg_baseline("rayleigh",
  pG = function(q, par, lower.tail = TRUE, log.p = FALSE) {
    lS <- ifelse(q > 0, -q^2 / (2 * par[["sigma"]]^2), 0)
    if (lower.tail) {
      p <- -expm1(lS)
      if (log.p) log(p) else p
    } else {
      if (log.p) lS else exp(lS)
    }
  },
  dG = function(x, par, log = FALSE) {
    s <- par[["sigma"]]
    d <- ifelse(x > 0, x / s^2 * exp(-x^2 / (2 * s^2)), 0)
    if (log) log(d) else d
  },
  qG = function(p, par) par[["sigma"]] * sqrt(-2 * log1p(-p)),
  par = c(sigma = 1), lower = 0, upper = Inf, support = c(0, Inf),
  start = function(x) c(sigma = sqrt(mean(x^2) / 2)))
rayleigh

set.seed(2)
z <- rbkwg(250, a = 2, b = 1, baseline = rayleigh, par = c(sigma = 2))
fit_bkwg(z, baseline = rayleigh, submodel = "EG")
```
